name: Mayotte
summary_text: Mayotte stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document rules, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules governing places of deprivation of liberty apply on the island as French law, and the French prison framework binds Mayotte's establishments as French prisons.  Nothing in that framework criminalises trans people or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been lawful on the island since the 1975 vote to remain within the Republic, and Mayotte is one of few jurisdictions in Africa and in the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed.  Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document rather than anatomy, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Reporting of 12 January 2018 documents that trans women incarcerated in France are accordingly held in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, and the French prison framework extends to local jails as French establishments.  France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that there is a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. That assessment rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections that interviewed eight trans women and one trans man at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; the establishments it covers include those on Mayotte.  The simplification of legal gender change voted by the French National Assembly is French law and therefore applies on Mayotte, giving trans residents access to the simplified civil-status procedure.  Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A report of 23 May 2023 describes a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner, pseudonym Abdallah, completing a long and complicated path before marrying at Sada Town Hall, in a predominantly Muslim society where the rights the law confers are not matched by social acceptance.

sources.title: Article 330 alinea 2 Penal Code - Mirguet amendment ordonnance of 1960 (repealed 1980)
sources.documents: Historical criminalisation of homosexual indecent exposure with doubled penalty; March 2024 National Assembly bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980.
sources.detail: No URL visible; cited as 1960 ordonnance proposed by Paul Mirguet, repealed in 1980 as part of act redefining sexual offenses; March 2024 compensation bill passed Assembly unanimously, pending Senate.

sources.title: French anti-discrimination legislation - 1985 law, July 2012 amendment, 18 November 2016 amendment to Article 225-1 Penal Code and Labour Code Chapter 2
sources.documents: Rights machinery: bans discrimination on sexual orientation (1985) and sexual identity/gender identity (2012, wording changed to 'gender identity' in 2016) in employment, housing, services; Labour Code text quoted.
sources.detail: No URL visible; cited as article 225-1 Penal Code amendment 18 November 2016 replacing 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity'; ILGA-Europe criticism noted.

sources.title: Law of 31 December 2004 amending anti-discrimination legislation and Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881 (Title 3, articles 20 and 21)
sources.documents: Hate-crime/speech enforcement machinery: criminalises homophobic/sexist/racist comments (45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months), creates Haute autorite de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'egalite; increased penalties when assault/murder motivated by sexual orientation.
sources.detail: No URL visible; cited with penalty maxima, Christian Vanneste conviction Jan 2006 later cancelled by Court of Cassation; Chirac Government justification of rise in anti-gay violence.

sources.title: Law of 18 November 2016 on legal gender change (effective 1 January 2017) + 2017 transphobia aggravation provision
sources.documents: Current transgender rights procedure: allows legal gender change without surgery/sterilisation or psychiatrist certificates via court (registry office for first name); 2017 law makes transphobia aggravating factor for imprisonable crimes.
sources.detail: No URL visible; legislative trail in text: Senate 6 Nov 2015, Assembly 24 May 2016, joint session 12 July 2016, Senate 28 Sept, Assembly 12 Oct, Constitutional Council 17 Nov, signed 18 Nov, published Journal Officiel next day.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe 2022 report on gender affirming healthcare in France; DILCRAH and 16 May 2020 Interior Ministry police victim data
sources.documents: Institutional monitoring and documented incidents: ILGA-Europe finds lack of self-determination, long waits, inequitable access; DILCRAH is Interministerial Delegation for Fight Against Racism, Anti-Semitism and Anti-LGBT Hatred; 2020 report shows 36% rise in 2019 with ~1,870 victims of homophobic/transphobic attacks vs ~1,380 in 2018.
sources.detail: No URL visible; cited as report published 2022, DILCRAH scientific committee controversy 2022 involving The Little Mermaid Observatory, and 16 May 2020 report released before IDAHOTB.
